title: The Exequy: occasion and publication
short: An elegy for King's first wife, Anne Berkeley, who died c. 1624 aged about 24; printed in King's Poems, Elegies, Paradoxes, and Sonnets (1657).
body: An 'exequy' is a funeral rite (Latin exsequiae, the procession that 'follows out' the dead). Henry King (1592-1669), later Bishop of Chichester, married Anne Berkeley around 1617; she died around 1624, leaving young children, and was buried in St Paul's. The poem circulated widely in manuscript (some copies are headed 'To his matchless never to be forgotten friend') before its printing in 1657. King was a close friend and executor of John Donne, and the poem's learned conceits (astronomy, alchemy, accounting, navigation) are in Donne's manner, though its tetrameter couplets are plainer and steadier. The archive's text is from an early print and has a few damaged letters (marked with ellipses).

title: Shrine ... Saint
short: The grave is a shrine and the dead wife a saint: the language of relics turned to private devotion.
body: A shrine was a reliquary or tomb holding a saint's remains. King addresses the tomb itself, an unusual move that he sustains later (ll. 61-78), where he speaks to the earth that holds his wife. Calling her a 'saint' means she is among the blessed in heaven, the same sense as in Milton's 'late espoused saint'. The idiom was safe for a Protestant cleric because it is metaphorical, but it carries the warmth of Catholic devotion.

title: strew
short: A 'strew' is a scattering: verses are thrown on the hearse instead of flowers.
body: Mourners strewed flowers on the coffin or hearse; King offers 'weeping verse' instead. The noun 'strew' (a number of things scattered about) is rare. 'Dirges' (l. 2) are funeral songs, from the first word of the antiphon Dirige, Domine in the Office of the Dead. 'Complaint' is the technical name for a poem of lament. 'Hearse' in the period could mean the framework over a coffin on which verses and tributes were pinned.

title: The book, the library
short: The dead wife is the only book he studies; 'Though almost blind' because his eyes are ruined by weeping.
body: Meditation on the dead was a recognised devotional exercise, and King makes his wife the text of that study: 'the book, / The library whereon I look'. The image matters for a scholar-cleric whose life was books. The paradox that he reads 'though almost blind' leads to the 'wet glasses' of line 15: his eyes, wet with tears, are like spectacles or hour-glasses through which he measures time.

title: wet glasses
short: His tear-filled eyes are 'glasses': perhaps hour-glasses that measure slow time, and lenses through which he looks.
body: The phrase works on two levels. Eyes as 'glasses' (lenses) continue the reading image; but the following lines ('How lazily time creeps about') suggest the hour-glass, with tears falling like sand. A further association with the water-clock (clepsydra) is possible. 'Compute the weary houres / With sighs dissolved into showres' (ll. 19-20) completes the conceit: sighs are wind, tears are rain, and time is measured in grief. 'Languish out' (l. 12) means to pass the days in languor.

title: preposterous
short: Literally 'before-behind': his time runs backward, with night coming at what should be his day.
body: The Latin praeposterus means 'the hinder part first', and seventeenth-century writers often used the word in that literal sense of inverted order. King's time is preposterous because darkness has come while it should still be day, and because the younger has died before the older. The theme returns at lines 105-110, where she has 'taken the field' before him.

title: benighted
short: She was his sun; her 'set' has brought night on him, an astronomical conceit that runs to the eclipse of lines 35-38.
body: 'Benighted' means overtaken by night. The wife is his day and his sun ('By thy cleer Sun / My love and fortune first did run'). The damaged word at the end of line 24 should read 'beget' (her setting begot an eve of blackness). The parenthesis 'though overcast / Before thou had'st thy Noon-tide past' notes that her life was clouded (by illness) before it reached its midday.

title: As day tells hours
short: She had scarcely lived as many years as there are hours in a day: about twenty-four, matching Anne King's age at death.
body: 'Tells' means counts (as a teller counts). The conceit equates her lifetime with a single day, so that her death at 'noon-tide' and the eve of blackness fit together. Biographical summaries give her age at death as about twenty-four; 'scarce' leaves the exact figure open. The line is a good example of how the poem's cosmic conceits keep returning to plain domestic fact.

title: my Hemisphere
short: His half of the sky, the part of the heavens visible to him, which her sun will never enter again.
body: In the old astronomy each observer sees one hemisphere of the heavens. She will never again rise into his. 'Light and motion' (l. 33) are the two properties of a star: she has lost both, 'like a fled Star', perhaps a shooting star or one of the new stars observed (and seen to vanish) in 1572 and 1604, which troubled ideas of unchanging heavens. The latter reference is suggestive rather than certain.

title: A strange eclipse ... Almanake
short: The earth between him and her makes an eclipse no almanac predicted: literally, she is buried, earth lies between them.
body: In a lunar eclipse the earth comes between sun and moon. Here 'the earth' between the speaker and his 'soul's dear wish' is the earth of the grave, so the astronomical figure becomes literal. Almanacs, very popular in the period, forecast eclipses; this one appears in none. The wit is in Donne's manner, but the effect is of controlled grief rather than display.

title: fad (sad) Clime
short: 'Fad' is a misprint or misreading of 'sad': in old type the long s (ſ) looks almost like f.
body: Early printing used the long s (ſ), which differs from f only by a missing crossbar; transcriptions often confuse them. Read 'my sad Clime'. 'Clime' means region or climate, continuing the astronomical-geographical language: she darkens his whole region of the world. Lines 39-48 imagine her absence as a temporary exile from which she might return, 'putting off thy ashy shrowd'.

title: calcine
short: An alchemical term: to burn to a fine powder, here the purging of the world by fire at the Last Judgement.
body: To calcine is to reduce a substance to powder (calx) by intense heat, a standard process in alchemy, where it was thought to purify by burning away grosser parts. At Doomsday the earth will be burnt 'to cinders' (compare 2 Peter 3:10, 'the elements shall melt with fervent heat'). The 'fierce Feaver' of the world's end is paralleled with the fever that killed his wife, so that her death becomes a small version of the apocalypse, and her resurrection a promise of the general one.

title: My Little World
short: The microcosm: a human being as a 'little world' mirroring the great world; her body, like the earth, must be purged by fire.
body: The idea that man is a microcosm (Greek mikros kosmos) corresponding part for part to the macrocosm was a Renaissance commonplace; Donne begins a Holy Sonnet 'I am a little world made cunningly'. King applies it tenderly to his wife: as the world will be calcined and renewed, so her feverish body will rise purified. 'Our bodies shall aspire / To our soules bliss' refers to the doctrine that the resurrected body rejoins the soul in heaven.

title: Doomsday book
short: The earth is told to inventory her body as William I's Domesday Book (1086) recorded every holding, and as the Judgement will account for all.
body: Lines 61-78 turn from astronomy to law and accountancy. The speaker addresses the earth as a trustee: he 'gives' it his short-lived 'right and interest' in her, but it must write each 'parcel' into its Doomsday book, make an exact 'reckoning', 'audit' every grain, and 'yield her back again by weight' at the resurrection. The Domesday Book was the great survey of England, nicknamed for its finality; King fuses it with the Day of Doom, when the dead are restored (Revelation 20:12-13). The legal tone, partly witty, also expresses an anxious love that wants none of her lost.

title: Casket
short: The grave as a jewel-box: she is a 'Rarity' laid up in the earth's casket.
body: 'Casket' means a small box for jewels or valuables (the sense of 'coffin' is later and American). The earth holds 'this Rarity' as treasure in trust, which continues the language of shrine and relic from the opening. 'Streight' (l. 73) means strict, exact. The two images, casket and Doomsday book, combine the language of the jewel-house and of the counting-house: she is both treasure and asset held in trust, to be returned intact.

title: Lent, not gave
short: God only lent her; the earth holds her in trust and must answer to Him: a Christian idea of life as a loan.
body: The distinction 'lent, / Not gave' expresses a common consolation: what God gives in this life is held on loan and may be recalled. 'Monument' (l. 78) here means something that keeps memory alive, a remembrance (RPO's gloss), not merely a tomb. The theological point is that her body belongs to God, and the earth is a steward, as in the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30), who must render an account.

title: Bride ... cold bed ... Marry my body
short: Burial as a wedding night: she is a bride put to bed, and he will be 'married' to the dust when he dies.
body: The closing movement turns funeral into marriage. Black curtains are drawn round her as round a bridal bed; 'Sleep on my Love in thy cold bed' and 'My last good night!' use the words of a husband at bedtime; and his own death will 'Marry my body to that dust / It so much loves'. Sleep as a figure for death is biblical (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14, 'them which sleep in Jesus'), and it implies waking at the resurrection.

title: that hallow (hollow) Vale
short: The grave, or the valley where the dead await judgement; texts divide between 'hollow' (the 1657 print) and 'hallow' (holy).
body: The RPO editor notes that manuscripts read 'hallow' where the printed text has 'hollow'; the archive's text has 'hallow'. 'Hollow vale' suggests the grave and the 'valley of the shadow of death' (Psalm 23:4); 'hallow vale' suggests a hallowed, consecrated place. Some readers also connect the vale with the valley of Jehoshaphat, where Joel imagines the nations gathered for judgement (Joel 3:2, 12), a link that is possible but not certain. 'Stay for me there' is among the most quoted lines in English elegy, praised for its quiet directness.

title: The voyage westward
short: Each night brings him eight hours' sail nearer the 'West' of life; his 'bottom' (ship) steers away from the sun toward death.
body: 'Bottom' means a ship's hull, so a ship (RPO glosses 'boat'). Each night's sleep carries him westward, toward sunset and death, 'almost by eight houres saile'. 'Each minute is a short degree' uses the navigator's degrees of longitude. 'Compass' means both the navigational instrument and the course or circuit of his days, which now 'downward bears'. He does not 'stem the tide' (steer against it) but glides with it toward her.

title: the Van ... my Pulse like a soft Drum
short: Military images: she, like the vanguard, took the field first; his pulse beats like a muffled drum marching him to join her.
body: 'Vann' is the van or vanguard, the front of an army, which engages first; she has won 'the victory' by dying first, although his greater age 'might crave / A just precedence'. The marching image continues: his pulse is a 'soft Drum' (muffled, as at military funerals) beating his approach, and however slow his 'marches', he 'shall at last sit down by Thee', 'sit down' being the military term for encamping before a town. The heartbeat as a funeral drum is one of the poem's most admired figures.

anchor: Divided, with but half a heart
title: The ending
short: He asks pardon for 'the crime' of being content to live on, half-hearted, until they meet 'and never part'.
body: The poem closes in hope rather than despair. 'Dissolution' is death (the soul's separation from the body; compare Philippians 1:23, 'having a desire to depart'). His 'crime' is consenting to live without her; the other half of his heart lies in her tomb (compare 'fill the room / My heart keeps empty in thy Tomb'). The last words, 'never part', answer the Christian hope of reunion and give the elegy its quiet resolution.

title: Metre and form
short: Iambic tetrameter couplets in verse paragraphs: a plain, steady measure that carries learned conceits without strain.
body: The poem is written in octosyllabic (four-stress) rhyming couplets, grouped into paragraphs of varying length. The short line keeps the poem moving and gives it the tone of speech, while the conceits drawn from astronomy, alchemy, law and navigation recall Donne. Many critics have praised the poem for combining metaphysical wit with deep, unforced feeling. Note the old spellings: 'Insteed', 'onely', 'cleer', 'ne're' (ne'er), 'heark' (hark).
